sources.headline: Why the US is bringing back firing squads
sources.text: Warning: this story contains upsetting descriptions of executionsAmerica's use of the death penalty is under the spotlight once again after US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that the military would livestream the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan.The former military psychiatrist fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at the Fort Hood military base in Texas in 2009.His execution would be the first time the US Army had used a firing squad since 1945, a method that several states already authorise to put people to death.And it comes on the heels of the botched death by lethal injection of Christa Pike - a woman convicted of murdering her classmate.Pike was taken to hospital and then discharged to prison 10 days later, after making a recovery from the failed attempt, her lawyers said.Amid rising concerns over botched executions - and renewed federal support for the death penalty - the US has introduced both new and old forms of execution like firing squads, the electric chair and the gas chamber.Lethal injection, which was first used in Texas in 1982, is now the most common way people are executed across the US, with many states making it their default method.Dr Joel Zivot, a professor of anaesthesiology and surgery based in Atlanta, Georgia, said states turned to lethal injection because it appeared from the outside to be a more peaceful means of execution."That was a myth," he said.Dr Zivot said that sometimes the injection of the drugs can cause pulmonary edema, when a person's lungs fill with fluid, which can give people the painful sensation of drowning."It's a terrifying way to die - to drown," he said.Other times, people have medical conditions, like Pike - who suffered from thrombocytosis and other medical problems her lawyers warned about - that can complicate the execution and make it more painful.During Pike's failed execution, "she could be heard crying, whimpering, and breathing loudly throughout the procedure", her lawyers said.There are a host of reasons why so many lethal injections have been botched, but some of the same factors persist, said Maher."Oftentimes, the executions go wrong because training of staff is inadequate, because drugs are degraded or expired or improperly stored, or because states are experimenting with different combinations of drugs that have never been used before," she said.In light of many of these challenges, some states have turned to executing people with a new and controversial method: nitrogen gas.Alabama and Louisiana are the first states to have carried out executions with nitrogen gas, though three other states - Arkansas, Mississippi and Oklahoma - also allow for it.Two years ago, Alabama used nitrogen gas to execute Kenneth Eugene Smith, after a botched attempt to put him to death via lethal injection in 2022.During the execution, which took 25 minutes, Smith thrashed violently on the gurney as he was given the gas, a witness told the BBC at the time.The method involves forcing a prisoner to breathe pure nitrogen gas until they suffocate.Dr Zivot said people who breathe in the gas sometimes get seizures. Alabama has executed seven people using nitrogen gas since introducing the method in January 2024."Each time it was a horror show of struggling, of moving, of seizing," Dr Zivot said.While some states have explored new methods, others have reauthorised some of the earliest ways US officials used to put people to death.As of this year, nine states have approved execution by electric chair, with South Carolina using it as their default method.Electrocution "has a horrible history of botched executions", Maher said, and errors with these executions is one of the reasons why states introduced lethal injections in the first place.In 1997, Pedro Medina's head caught fire as he was put to death in an electric chair in Florida."A solid flame covered his whole head, from one side to the other. I had the impression of somebody being burned alive," his attorney Mike Minerva said, according to the Los Angeles Times.A method once used as punishment in the military and in times of war, firing squad executions have also proven susceptible to human error.Mikahl Mahdi was executed by a three-person firing squad last year after admitting to killing an off-duty police officer in 2004. But his lawyers say his death was prolonged because the bullets missed his heart and instead hit his liver and other organs.In July, Idaho became the first state to use a firing squad as its primary method of execution after it ran into issues with lethal injections. Mississippi, Oklahoma, Utah and South Carolina also authorise this execution method.Alonzo Lunsford, a former US Army sergeant who survived being shot seven times by Hasan in the Fort Hood attack, told the BBC the firing squad was a "befitting" method to end his life because lethal injection and a gas chamber would be "doing him a favour".Hanging was the main method of execution in the US until the 1890s, and several Asian countries including Japan and Singapore still use this method. But in the US, no states authorise hanging because of its "terrible" history, Maher said."Hanging has such a terrible association with racial violence and lynching in the states," she said. "So that is why there's no state that's using hanging or has authorised that method to be used."Trump - a proponent of the death penalty - brought back the federal death penalty when he returned to office in 2025, after Joe Biden's administration put a moratorium on federal executions in 2021."Capital punishment is an essential tool for deterring and punishing those who would commit the most heinous crimes and acts of lethal violence against American citizens," his office wrote in an executive order.Maher said there has been "quite a bit of activity" in state legislatures to approve and reauthorise other methods of execution since Trump began expressing enthusiasm for the death penalty.Trump has called for the death penalty to be expanded to punish large-scale drug dealers, human traffickers and those who kill police officers. Over the past 50 years, all prisoners who received death sentences were convicted of murder, though capital punishment was also used for rape convictions before that.Asked by reporters whether Pike's failed lethal injection should spur changes to the death penalty, Trump did not directly answer the question, adding that the execution method "shouldn't be very difficult".

sources.headline: Australia may risk a diplomatic spat with the Trump administration if it limits the viewing of a US execution
sources.text: Australia’s online safety regulator has a few levers to limit the public seeing the US’s planned live stream of an execution but history suggests it will lead to a very public fight.The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, announced last week the planned execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan would be livestreamed when the military execution is carried out in early December.The Greens have called on the eSafety commissioner, Julie Inman Grant, and the Albanese government to ensure that the event – if it goes ahead and is livestreamed – is not seen by Australians on TV or their devices.The eSafety commissioner, under the Online Safety Act, has powers to order platforms such as Facebook, Instagram and X to block Australians from accessing posts that contain content deemed to be “refused classification” under Australian classification law.The classification of such extreme violent material is typically applied to content online of terror attacks, and other terror-related content, but it could be applied to clips of the video of the public execution after the fact.While some companies such as Meta will probably apply their own terms of service and prevent the distribution of the video, history suggests others will take a stand that the video should remain on their platforms.X has given no indication whether it will allow such videos but the platform owned by Elon Musk has a long history of legal challenges against eSafety when it comes to this sort of content.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereIn 2024, X was successful in allowing footage of the stabbing of a Sydney bishop in his church in 2024 to remain available to Australians – the platform even recruited the bishop, Mar Mari Emmanuel, to argue to the court to allow the footage to stay online.Most recently, X won an appeal to the classifications review board to have the classification of the video of the assassination of rightwing influencer Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University downgraded from RC to R18+, after eSafety ordered the removal of clips of the assassination last year.It also won a similar case to reduce the rating of videos of the attack on Iryna Zarutska on a train in Charlotte, North Carolina, in August last year down to R18+.In laws passed by the former Coalition government in 2019 after the Christchurch terror attack, the eSafety commissioner also has powers to issue takedown notices to websites hosting footage that, among other things, depicts “actual violent crime such as murder, attempted murder, rape, torture”.These laws were developed with the view to block streaming of terror attacks but could have wider applications for state-sponsored violence such as executions.The eSafety commissioner last used these powers in 2022 to order websites to remove videos and related materials of the Buffalo, New York, terrorist attack in 2022. It can also declare an “online crisis event” and order internet service providers such as Telstra and Optus to block sites hosting the content, but this power has yet to be used.The ISPs complied with eSafety’s request to block sites hosting the Christchurch attack in 2019 before the parliament had passed the laws.skip past newsletter promotionafter newsletter promotionSuch a move – particularly if focused on large social media platforms, or potentially sites owned by the Trump administration – may lead to a domestic firestorm among conservative media as well as a potential diplomatic incident, and may not be the regulator’s preferred option – especially given it has not been used before.Last, there is the potential to seek penalties against platforms that fail to detect and remove violent material from their platform. The regulator is now testing this law out with messaging platform Telegram, which eSafety has alleged failed to remove some content that included executions conducted by terrorist groups.The eSafety commissioner is seeking fines of up to A$54.6m and the hearing for the case is set down for February next year.The other factor to consider is the laser-focus some in the US already have on Inman Grant. Her term is up in January next year, and Inman Grant has previously said she will not seek another term, but Trump-aligned politicians such as the Republican congressman Jim Jordan have labelled Inman Grant as a “zealot for global takedowns” and claimed she has threatened American speech on social media platforms.Inman Grant has rejected the claims and she declined an invitation to speak before a US congress hearing at the time.If Inman Grant bears the responsibility for decisions around whether Australians can see the livestreamed execution, it will likely provoke a new round of criticism.The regulator late on Monday said it did not have powers to proactively block the streaming in Australia, and said it would monitor and enforce existing standards that could obligate online platforms to block it themselves.The history of legal challenges and attention from the right of politics in the US suggests no easy solution in the eSafety toolkit – short of ministerial intervention.

Catholics in US Army must not take part in firing squad, armed forces archbishop says

Army cleric Timothy Broglio has objected to the Pentagon’s plan to live stream the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan in December

Published: 4:41am, 13 Oct 2026

Catholics serving in the US Army should not take part in the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan that the Pentagon is planning to live stream on December 3, a prominent US archbishop said on Monday.

In an unusually strongly worded statement, Archbishop Timothy Broglio, who oversees the spiritual care of ‌Catholic members of the US armed forces, raised a series of objections to the unprecedented plan to broadcast the execution of Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in a 2009 shooting spree.

Broglio said he presided at the funeral of one of Hasan’s victims and lamented the shooting. But the Ohio-born archbishop asked whether the US wanted to “imitate the terrorists of this world and make a public spectacle of barbarically killing our adversaries”.

“I oblige any Catholics assigned to ⁠the firing squad to request to be excused from this action contrary to the teaching of the church,” Broglio said.

US Army regulations do ‌allow for soldiers to request religious exemptions or accommodations and the army has yet to say how it intends to select members of the firing squad.

US Defence Secretary Pete ‌Hegseth announced plans to live stream the shooting last week, triggering a backlash among Republicans in Congress, religious leaders and ⁠international observers. US President Donald ⁠Trump approved Hasan’s execution by firing squad but has said he is still deciding whether to allow the live streaming to proceed.

The event would be extraordinary, even for ‌a country that has long employed capital punishment. A government execution has never been broadcast or live streamed, according to death penalty experts, and the US military has not executed anyone ‌by ‌firing squad since 1945. Hasan, now 56, requires a wheelchair, having been shot by police during his arrest.

Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas in a 2009 shooting spree, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on December 3. Photo: Bell County Sheriff’s Office / Handout / Reuters

Hegseth said last week he ‌wants US soldiers to execute Hasan at the time, day of the week and location of Hasan’s shooting spree. Hegseth has argued ⁠that making the event public will help serve as a deterrent.

Broglio questioned whether the effect of a live streamed execution on young viewers ⁠had been considered. He said the US military had a good reputation and asked if there was “really a value to throwing them in the same boat with terrorists by broadcasting the image of the execution of a man ‌in a wheelchair to the whole world”.

Broglio’s ‌statement was issued soon after he met Pope Leo in Rome on Monday. Leo has clashed with Trump and his Pentagon over issues including the Iran war. Leo on Saturday condemned the death penalty, without mentioning the Hasan case specifically.

US Vice-President J.D. Vance, a convert to Catholicism, has said that if it does ultimately get live streamed, he would not watch it.

sources.headline: 'No elevated risk’: US homeland security chief defends plan to livestream Nidal Hasan’s execution
sources.text: FILE PHOTO: Nidal HasanUS Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has defended the Trump administration’s plan to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, the former US Army major convicted of killing 13 soldiers at Fort Hood in Texas, dismissing concerns that the broadcast could fuel radicalisation or turn him into a martyr.“I don’t see an elevated risk at this point at all because of this,” Mullin said in an interview with CBS News’ Face the Nation on Sunday.“If you attack America, we will come after you, and we will make sure that the punishment fits the crime,” he added.Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on December 3 for the 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, in which 13 people were killed and 32 others injured.The plan to broadcast his execution live, announced by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth last week, has drawn criticism from both Republicans and Democrats. President Donald Trump has backed the idea but has not made a final decision on whether the execution will be televised.Mullin said the administration had considered the potential risks and argued that viewers would not be forced to watch the broadcast.“No one has to watch it if they don’t choose to,” he told CBS News.However, critics have warned that broadcasting the execution could give extremist groups propaganda material and increase security risks for Americans at home and abroad.Alaska Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski called the proposal “gruesome”, arguing that it could give Hasan the martyrdom he sought.“It's something I would expect from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America,” she wrote on X, adding that the way the US carries out justice matters as much as the justice itself.Virginia Democratic Senator Mark Warner also cautioned that a public execution could provide terrorist organisations with a propaganda victory, fuel radicalisation and put American service members, diplomats and citizens overseas at greater risk.Hasan, who was shot during the attack and now uses a wheelchair, admitted to killing the unarmed troops at a crowded medical facility at Fort Hood. During his trial, he said he believed he was protecting Muslims and the Taliban in Afghanistan from the US military.If carried out, Hasan’s execution would be the first by the US military since 1961 and its first firing-squad execution since World War II. A public broadcast would also mark the first public execution in the United States in nearly a century.

sources.headline: Pope says death penalty "inadmissible" amid U.S. plans to livestream execution
sources.text:
October 10, 2026 / 11:28 AM EDT
/ CBS/AP
Add CBS News on Google
Pope Leo XIV declared that capital punishment is "inadmissible" as the United States plans to livestream an execution by firing squad.The American pope, in a post on X marking the World Day Against the Death Penalty, quoted the revised Catholic teaching on capital punishment ushered in by his predecessor, Pope Francis. The Catholic teaching states that capital punishment attacks the inherent dignity of a human being."The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment," read the post under Leo's official handle, @Pontifex. "Effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption."The U.S. Defense Department announced Thursday that the firing squad execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of a 2009 shooting at the Fort Hood military base, will be livestreamed. Hasan, scheduled to be executed at Fort Hood on Dec. 3, was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others. It would be the first U.S. military execution since 1961.The decision to livestream the execution has drawn fierce criticism. Leo's post didn't refer specifically to the planned execution in the U.S. or the botched lethal injection of Christa Pike in Tennessee late last month which has revived debate over the death penalty in the United States. However, it is common for the pope's official social media accounts to post messages marking such commemorations like the World Day Against the Death Penalty.However, Leo's post came just hours after his top deputy, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said explicitly that the planned U.S. public execution was "unacceptable."
Speaking specifically about the United States, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, said the planned livestreamed execution was "truly incomprehensible" and "unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle.""The Church's position is one of total opposition to the death penalty; it is incompatible with human dignity and serves as no deterrent… ," Parolin said in comments carried by Vatican News. "It is truly incomprehensible that anyone would want to use this system today — I don't know for what purpose. It is certainly unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle; even if the person is guilty, of course, there are other methods."The head of the U.S. bishops conference, Archbishop Paul Coakley, expressed "shock" and "great sorrow" at the Pentagon's plans."In no way can Hasan's actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," he said in a statement Friday. "The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people."
On Friday, President Trump said he approves of Hasan's execution by firing squad."He will be killed. He will be, through firing squad," Mr. Trump told reporters before flying to Syracuse, New York, for a political event. "I really don't care how he goes, as long as he goes. And I think the death penalty is a very worthy way of going for him."Mr. Trump did not appear to answer when asked whether it was appropriate to livestream the event or whether he was going to watch the execution.Vice President JD Vance, who is a Catholic convert, appeared to cast doubt on Friday about the livestream, telling reporters he wouldn't watch it and, "I don't know that that's actually going to happen."

Pope Leo XIV
